intro: In the 1800s, many Americans belonged to secret societies. Many others feared them. This unit shows what happened when that fear grew. It starts with a man who vanished from a New York jail in 1826. It moves to a Chicago street clash over beer licenses in 1855. It ends with a fake oath that showed up in the records of Congress in 1913.

Each story has real people at its center. There is a missing man and his family. There are immigrant families who wanted to work and live in peace. There are neighbors blamed for plots they never joined. And there are people who spoke up, like an Illinois lawyer who wrote honestly to a friend, and a committee that named a forgery for what it was.

By the end of this unit, you will be able to sort what records prove from what people only claimed. You will explain how the Morgan affair changed American elections. You will describe the Know-Nothings and the Lager Beer Riot. You will also be able to spot when a real document is used to mislead.
bigQuestion: When Americans feared secret societies, what did they get right, what did they get wrong, and who paid the price?

timeline.t: Morgan's book, Illustrations of Masonry, is filed for copyright in New York
Morgan is arrested, jailed at Canandaigua and taken away at night; he is never seen again
Four men are convicted at Canandaigua for their part in the kidnapping
A body found at Oak Orchard Creek is claimed as Morgan's but named as Timothy Munroe
The Anti-Masons hold the first national nominating convention, in Baltimore
Anti-Masonic candidate William Wirt wins Vermont's 7 electoral votes
Charles B. Allen starts the Order of the Star Spangled Banner in New York City
Chicago's Lager Beer Riot follows Mayor Levi Boone's new saloon rules
Millard Fillmore runs for president for the American Party and wins only Maryland
Jonathan Blanchard's National Christian Association starts the Christian Cynosure in Chicago
The Knights of Columbus are chartered, and the Morgan Monument is dedicated in Batavia
A House committee condemns a forged Knights of Columbus oath as false

words.d: a piece of writing that reveals something a group wanted kept hidden
a solemn promise, often made before God
taking a person away by force
taking and holding a person by force
people who opposed the Masonic order, especially after the Morgan affair
a political party outside the two main parties
a meeting where a political party picks its candidate
the belief that people born in a country deserve more rights than newcomers
members of the secret Order of the Star Spangled Banner and the movement it led in the 1850s
cutting back on alcohol or banning it
a fake made to look real
the facts around something that give it meaning

test.q: What was William Morgan's book, Illustrations of Masonry, meant to reveal?
choices: The secret rituals of the Freemasons
The route of the Erie Canal
test.why: Morgan's exposé promised to print the Masons' secret words, signs and ceremonies.

test.q: Why was no one convicted of murdering Morgan?
choices: No one could prove he was dead
Murder trials were not allowed in New York
test.why: No body was ever confirmed as Morgan's, so the men were convicted of kidnapping, not murder.

test.q: What was new about the Anti-Masonic meeting in Baltimore in 1831?
choices: It was the first time Masons met in public
It closed every lodge in Maryland
It was the first national nominating convention
test.why: The Anti-Masons held the first national nominating convention, and other parties copied the idea.

test.q: According to his widow, whose body was found at Oak Orchard Creek in 1827?
test.why: A widow said the body was her husband, Timothy Munroe, and it was named as Munroe.

test.q: Which statement about the Morgan affair is documented?
choices: Men were convicted of kidnapping him
The whole Masonic order planned his death
He was drowned in Lake Erie
He was seen alive in Chicago
test.why: Court records show men were convicted of kidnapping. The other claims were never proven.

test.q: What does the 1882 Morgan Monument teach about monuments?
choices: They are always checked by courts
They can state beliefs as facts that were never proven
They are always paid for by the government
They list every member of a lodge
test.why: The monument says Masons murdered Morgan, a claim no court ever proved.

test.q: What did the Anti-Masons and the Know-Nothings have in common?
choices: Both turned fear of a group into a political movement
test.why: The Anti-Masons turned fear of Masons into a party, and the Know-Nothings turned fear of Catholic immigrants into the American Party.

test.q: On the surface, what was the Lager Beer Riot about?
choices: Saloon license fees and Sunday closing
test.why: Chicago raised the saloon license fee from $50 to $300 and moved to close saloons on Sundays.

test.q: Which group had the most to lose from Mayor Boone's saloon rules?
choices: German and Irish immigrant saloon keepers
test.why: Many saloons and beer halls were run by German and Irish immigrants, so the rules hit them hardest.

test.q: What did Lincoln warn about in his 1855 letter to Joshua Speed?
choices: He wanted to rewrite the Constitution
He said the Know-Nothings would add exceptions to the promise that all men are created equal
He said the Declaration should stay secret
He said the Declaration applied only to Illinois
test.why: Lincoln warned that Know-Nothings would make the Declaration exclude Black people, foreigners and Catholics.

test.q: Why did Jonathan Blanchard oppose secret societies?
choices: He wanted to start his own lodge
He was paid by the Know-Nothings
He believed secret oaths were wrong for Christians and for a free country
He had been kidnapped by Masons
test.why: Blanchard's reasons were religious and political: no secret oaths, and open dealing in a free country.

test.q: Why did Father McGivney start the Knights of Columbus?
choices: To oppose the Masons in court
To give Catholic men a fraternal order and protect families with insurance
test.why: McGivney wanted a Catholic brotherhood that would help families, including widows and children.

test.q: Which fact shows most clearly that the 1913 Knights of Columbus oath was not real?
choices: A House committee condemned it as false and libelous
It was printed on cheap paper
test.why: The House committee that studied the case called the oath false, spurious and libelous.

test.q: A pamphlet quotes a real document but leaves out that the document called its words false. What is this an example of?
choices: Using a source out of context
test.why: Leaving out the facts around a quotation gives readers a false idea. That is using a source out of context.

test.q: Which is a fair conclusion from the whole unit?
choices: Fears about secret groups were always right
No one ever stood up to false fears
Fear of secret groups was often turned against ordinary people who had done nothing wrong
test.why: Masons, Catholic immigrants and Catholic Knights were each blamed for plots most of them never joined.

write.prompt: Was the fear of secret societies between 1826 and 1913 mostly fair or mostly unfair? Choose one case from the unit. Cite two or three facts or sources, and explain your claim.

Keep what records prove apart from what people only claimed.
Give the other side fairly before you answer it.
Use at least three words from this unit, such as nativism, forgery or context.

title: America Fears the Secret Societies

chapters.title: The Disappearance of William Morgan
chapters.bigQuestion: How did one man's disappearance in 1826 change the way Americans felt about secret societies and politics?

story.title: A Carriage in the Dark
story.kicker: On a September night in 1826, a man walks out of a small-town jail in New York and is never seen again.
paragraphs: It is the night of September 12, 1826. The town of Canandaigua, in western New York, is dark and quiet. Inside the county jail sits a man named William Morgan. He is there because he owes a small debt to an innkeeper, less than three dollars. Two days ago he was at home in the town of Batavia, about fifty miles to the west.

Morgan has made some people very angry. He has been working on a book. It promises to print the secret ceremonies of the Freemasons, a brotherhood with lodges in almost every town. Many Masons feel he is breaking a solemn promise. Some of them are furious.

That night, men come to the jail and pay what Morgan owes. He is let out into the dark. Witnesses later say he struggled and called for help. He is put into a waiting carriage. The carriage rolls west toward Fort Niagara, where the Niagara River separates New York from Canada.

William Morgan was never seen again. No one has ever proved what happened to him. But his disappearance set off a storm. Within a few years, hundreds of Masonic lodges closed. A new political party was born. Even the way Americans choose candidates for president changed.
story.think: Why might a mystery with no clear answer make people angrier than a crime that is solved in court?

lessons.title: Morgan's Book Plan
lessons.mainIdea: In 1826 William Morgan of Batavia, New York, planned to publish a book revealing Masonic rituals, and that plan put him in danger.
reading: Batavia was a small town in western New York in 1826. The Erie Canal had opened the year before, and towns across the region were growing fast. William Morgan lived in Batavia with his wife and young children. He had taken part in Masonic lodge meetings. Now he had a different plan.

Morgan teamed up with a Batavia printer named David C. Miller. Together they planned a book called Illustrations of Masonry. On August 14, 1826, the title was filed for copyright. The book promised to print the secret words, signs and ceremonies that Masons used in their lodges.

A book like this is called an *exposé*. An exposé reveals something a group wanted kept hidden. Exposés of Masonry were not new. One had been printed in London almost a hundred years earlier. But in a small town where everyone knew each other, this one felt personal.

Each Masonic ceremony followed a *ritual*. A ritual is a set of words and actions done the same way each time. For Masons, rituals marked each step a member took in the brotherhood. Many members felt that printing them was a betrayal.

words.d: a piece of writing that reveals something a group wanted kept hidden
a set of words and actions done the same way each time, often in a ceremony

look.title: A Printer's Shop in Batavia
look.text: Picture a small printing shop in 1826. Sheets of damp paper hang drying on a line. A printer sets tiny metal letters, one by one, into a frame. A man beside him reads aloud from handwritten pages about passwords and handshakes. Both men know that many of their neighbors will be angry when the book comes out.
look.prompt: Why might a writer and a printer take this risk? List one reason they might have had and one danger they faced.

check.q: What did William Morgan plan to publish in 1826?
choices: A map of the Erie Canal
A newspaper for a new political party
check.why: The reading says Morgan planned Illustrations of Masonry, which promised to print the Masons' secret words, signs and ceremonies.

check.q: What is an exposé?
choices: A secret handshake used in a lodge
A promise made in a ceremony
A piece of writing that reveals what a group wanted hidden
A court order to free a prisoner
check.why: An exposé reveals something a group wanted kept hidden, as Morgan's book tried to do.

check.q: Who worked with Morgan on the book?
check.why: The reading says Morgan teamed up with David C. Miller, a printer in Batavia.

lessons.title: Promises Inside the Lodge
lessons.mainIdea: Masons saw their secret signs and promises as a sign of trust, while critics saw secret oaths as a danger to fair government.
reading: Imagine joining a club where members help each other's families when times are hard. To join, you make a serious promise to keep the club's words and signs private. In the 1820s, many thousands of American men belonged to clubs like this. The best known was the Freemasons.

Masons met in a *lodge*. The word means both the local group and the room where it meets. Members were farmers, shopkeepers, lawyers and judges. They said the lodge taught good character and charity. They said the secret signs helped them trust a brother Mason from another town.

To join, a man took an *oath*. An oath is a solemn promise, often made before God. Masonic oaths promised to keep the lodge's secrets. Some oaths named harsh penalties for breaking the promise. Masons said these penalties were symbols of how serious the promise was.

Critics saw the same oaths differently. They asked: what if a Mason's promise to his lodge came before his duty to the law? What if a judge or a juror favored a brother Mason? After Morgan vanished, that question swept across the country.

words.d: a local group of Masons, and also the room where they meet
a solemn promise, often made before God

look.title: Two Ways to See One Promise
look.text: A lodge member says: My oath means my brothers can trust me, and I will help their widows and children. A critic says: A secret oath could make a man protect his brothers even when they break the law. Both speakers are talking about the very same promise.
look.prompt: What does each speaker care about most? What facts would you want before deciding which view fits a real case?

check.q: What is an oath?
choices: A secret password for a meeting
A room where a club meets
A book that reveals a club's secrets
A solemn promise, often made before God
check.why: The reading defines an oath as a solemn promise, often made before God. Masons took one when they joined.

check.q: According to the reading, why did Masons say their secret signs were useful?
choices: They helped members trust a brother Mason from another town
They were needed to enter churches
They let members skip paying debts
check.why: Masons said the signs helped them trust a brother Mason from another town.

check.q: What worry did critics have about Masonic oaths?
choices: That the oaths were written in Latin
That a Mason might favor his lodge brothers over the law
That the oaths cost too much money
That children had to take the oaths too
check.why: Critics asked whether a Mason's promise to his lodge might come before his duty to the law.

lessons.title: Arrested and Jailed
lessons.mainIdea: Morgan was arrested on September 11, 1826, on a small theft charge that was dropped, and then he was held in the Canandaigua jail for a tiny debt.
reading: On September 11, 1826, officers arrested William Morgan. The *charge* was petty theft, over a shirt and a tie. A charge is a formal claim that a person broke the law. A charge is not proof. It still has to be shown in court.

Morgan was taken about fifty miles east to the jail at Canandaigua. There the theft charge was dropped. For a moment he was free. Then he was arrested again. This time it was for a *debt* of about $2.69 that he owed an innkeeper.

Why does this matter? A debt of less than three dollars was a small sum, even in 1826. Many people later believed the charges were a trick. They thought someone wanted Morgan locked up far from home, away from his friends and his printer.

The arrests themselves are well recorded. Whether they were planned as a trap is a harder question. It fits what happened next. People who study the case still weigh how much was planned ahead, and by whom.

words.d: a formal claim that a person broke the law; it is not proof
money that a person owes to someone else

look.title: Two Days in Order
look.text: September 11: Morgan is arrested for petty theft. He is taken to Canandaigua. The theft charge is dropped. He is jailed again for a debt of about $2.69. September 12, at night: men pay the debt, and Morgan walks out of the jail.
look.prompt: Look at the order of events. Which step seems most surprising to you? Why might people have become suspicious?

check.q: Where was Morgan held after his arrest?
check.why: The reading says Morgan was taken about fifty miles east to the jail at Canandaigua.

check.q: What happened to the theft charge?
choices: It led to a two-year sentence
It was proven by a jury
check.why: At Canandaigua the theft charge was dropped, and Morgan was then jailed for a small debt.

check.q: Why did many people think the arrests were a trick?
choices: Morgan had never been to Batavia
The charges were small and kept him far from home
check.why: The charges were tiny, and they kept Morgan locked up far from his friends and his printer.

lessons.title: Taken in the Night
lessons.mainIdea: On the night of September 12, 1826, men paid Morgan's debt and took him from the jail by carriage toward Fort Niagara, and he was never seen again.
reading: On the night of September 12, a group of men came to the Canandaigua jail. They paid Morgan's small debt, so the jail let him go. Outside, he was put into a carriage. Witnesses later said he struggled and called for help.

Taking a person away by force is called *abduction*. The carriage traveled west across New York. Its goal was Fort Niagara, an old fort where the Niagara River flows into Lake Ontario. Canada lies just across the river.
Reports later said Morgan was held at the fort for a short time. After that, the trail goes cold. No one has ever produced a confirmed record of where he went or what happened to him.

Several parts of that night are *documented*, which means written records support them. The arrest, the jail, the paid debt and the carriage ride are all documented. His fate is not. That gap between the known and the unknown is where rumors grew.

words.d: taking a person away by force
supported by written records or other solid evidence

look.title: A Route Across New York
look.text: Trace a line on a map of New York. Start at Batavia. Move east to Canandaigua and its jail. Then turn and travel far west, past Batavia again, to Fort Niagara. There the Niagara River flows into Lake Ontario, and Canada lies just across the water.
look.prompt: Why might the men have chosen a place on the border with Canada? What does the route suggest, and what does it not prove?

check.q: What is an abduction?
choices: Paying off a debt for someone
Choosing a candidate at a meeting
Taking a person away by force
check.why: The reading defines abduction as taking a person away by force, as happened to Morgan.

check.q: Where was the carriage headed?
choices: Fort Niagara, on the border with Canada
check.why: The carriage went west toward Fort Niagara, where the Niagara River meets Lake Ontario across from Canada.

check.q: Which part of the story is NOT documented?
choices: The paid debt at the jail
The carriage ride from the jail
check.why: The reading says the arrest, jail, debt and carriage ride are documented, but his fate is not.

lessons.title: What Happened to Morgan?
lessons.mainIdea: No one has ever proved what happened to Morgan; people offered several theories, and the evidence does not settle them.
reading: Soon after Morgan vanished, people started to guess. Some said he was drowned in the Niagara River. Others said he was paid to leave the country and start a new life. Over the years, stories claimed he had been seen alive in faraway places.

Each guess is a *theory*, an idea that tries to explain what happened. A strong theory fits the evidence. A weak theory asks you to ignore some facts or to trust a rumor. A *rumor* is a story passed from person to person without proof.

The strongest evidence shows that Morgan was taken against his will by men linked to local lodges. It does not show what happened after Fort Niagara. No body was ever confirmed as his. No court ever found anyone guilty of killing him.
Many people believed, then and now, that he was killed. Many Masons argued that a few angry men had done the crime, not the whole order. Historians still treat his fate as an open question.

words.d: an idea that tries to explain what happened
a story passed from person to person without proof

look.title: Sort the Claims
look.text: Claim A: Men took Morgan from the Canandaigua jail by carriage. Claim B: Morgan was drowned in the Niagara River. Claim C: Morgan was paid to move far away. Claim D: Some of the men who took part were tried in court.
look.prompt: Sort each claim into two piles, documented or unproven. What kind of evidence would move a claim from one pile to the other?

check.q: What is a theory?
choices: A story passed along with no proof
An idea that tries to explain what happened
check.why: A theory is an idea that tries to explain what happened. People had several theories about Morgan.

check.q: According to the reading, what did no court ever do?
choices: Find anyone guilty of killing Morgan
Hold any trial about the case
check.why: The reading says no court ever found anyone guilty of killing Morgan.

check.q: Which statement fits the evidence best?
choices: Morgan was proven to have drowned
Morgan was taken against his will, and his fate is unknown
Morgan's body was buried in Batavia
check.why: The evidence shows he was taken against his will, but it does not show what happened next.

lessons.title: A Body at Oak Orchard Creek
lessons.mainIdea: In 1827 a body was claimed to be Morgan's, but a widow said it was her husband, which shows how people can bend evidence to fit what they want.
reading: In October 1827, more than a year after Morgan vanished, a body was found near Oak Orchard Creek, by Lake Ontario. People who blamed the Masons quickly said it was Morgan. At last, they said, here was proof of murder.
Then a widow came forward. She said the body was her husband, Timothy Munroe, who had drowned. In the end, the body was named as Munroe, not Morgan. The proof that people had hoped for was gone.

A newspaper editor named Thurlow Weed was a leader of the *Anti-Masons*, people who opposed the Masonic order. His critics said he used the body to win votes. Two versions of what Weed said about the body survive, and they paint him very differently.

This is a lesson about *evidence*, the facts that help show whether a claim is true. When people badly want a story to be true, they may grab any clue that seems to fit. A careful reader asks: who is making the claim, what do they gain, and what does other evidence show?

words.d: people who opposed the Masonic order, especially after the Morgan affair
facts or objects that help show whether a claim is true

look.title: Two Versions of One Remark
look.text: The popular version: Weed said the body was a good enough Morgan until after the election. Weed's own version: when told it was not Morgan, he said it was good enough for them until the Masons brought back the man they had carried off.
look.cite: Popular accounts of the Morgan affair, and Thurlow Weed's own account in his autobiography, published 1883 (both paraphrased)
look.prompt: How does each version make Weed look? Why might Weed's own account and his critics' account be different?

check.q: Who did the widow say the body was?
check.why: The widow said the body was her husband, Timothy Munroe, and it was named as Munroe.

check.q: Who were the Anti-Masons?
choices: A group of printers in Batavia
People who opposed the Masonic order
check.why: The reading defines Anti-Masons as people who opposed the Masonic order.

check.q: Why does the reading call the body story a lesson about evidence?
choices: It shows people may grab a clue that fits what they want to believe
It shows newspapers never make mistakes
It proves Weed was a Mason
check.why: People who wanted proof of murder claimed the body too quickly, before the evidence was weighed.

lessons.title: Trials and Short Sentences
lessons.mainIdea: Several men were convicted of kidnapping Morgan, but their sentences ranged only from one month to 28 months.
reading: In January 1827, a court at Canandaigua tried four men named Lawson, Chesebro, Sawyer and Sheldon for their part in taking Morgan. All four were *convicted*, which means found guilty. The crime was *kidnapping*, taking and holding a person by force. Without a body, no one could prove Morgan was dead.

Their sentences were short. A *sentence* is the punishment a court gives. Lawson got two years. Chesebro got one year. Sheldon got three months. Sawyer got one month. None of them was sent away for long.

Later, Eli Bruce, the sheriff of Niagara County, was also convicted. He served 28 months in the Canandaigua jail. New York's governor, DeWitt Clinton, removed him from office. Other men were tried in the years that followed.
To many people, the punishments seemed far too small. A man had vanished, and the longest sentence was just over two years. That feeling of unfairness turned shock into public anger.

words.d: found guilty of a crime by a court
taking and holding a person by force
the punishment a court gives to a person found guilty

look.title: Sentences in the Morgan Kidnapping Cases
look.cite: Court results of 1827-1828 as given in Charles F. Milliken, A History of Ontario County, New York, and Its People (1911), and The Masonic Martyr, a biography of Eli Bruce
look.prompt: How many times longer was the sheriff's sentence than Sawyer's? Why might people expect a public official to be punished more?

check.q: What does convicted mean?
check.why: Convicted means found guilty of a crime by a court, as the four men were in 1827.

check.q: What was the longest sentence in the Morgan cases?
choices: 28 months, served by Sheriff Eli Bruce
check.why: Sheriff Eli Bruce served 28 months, which was longer than Lawson's two years.

check.q: Why were the men charged with kidnapping, not murder?
choices: Without a body, no one could prove Morgan was dead
Murder was not a crime in 1827
Morgan asked the court to go easy
check.why: The reading says that without a body, no one could prove Morgan was dead.

lessons.title: Why the Public Grew Angry
lessons.mainIdea: People grew angry because they suspected Masons in public office had protected each other, even though most Masons had no part in the crime.
reading: Picture a farmer in western New York in 1828. He hears that a man was taken from a jail. He hears that a sheriff helped. He hears that the punishments were small. He starts to wonder who else knew. Many of his neighbors wonder too.

Critics pointed to a pattern. Some officials in the Morgan cases were Masons. Some trials ended with men *acquitted*, or found not guilty. To critics, this looked like a *cover-up*, an effort to hide the truth and protect the guilty.

Masons answered that a small group of men had done the crime. Most Masons had nothing to do with it. They pointed out that Governor Clinton, himself a well-known Mason, removed the sheriff who took part.

Both sides had a point. There was a real crime and there were real reasons for doubt. There was also real unfairness in blaming every member for what a few had done. When a group is secret, it is hard for its members to show outsiders they are innocent. That made the anger last.

words.d: found not guilty by a court
an effort to hide the truth and protect the people responsible

look.title: Two Imagined Letters to the Editor
look.text: Letter 1: A sheriff helped take a man from a jail, and the punishments were tiny. Masons in office protect their own. Letter 2: I am a Mason and a farmer. I never heard of this plot until I read the paper. Why am I treated like a criminal?
look.prompt: Which facts from the lesson support each letter? What would be a fair way to answer both writers?

check.q: What is a cover-up?
choices: An effort to hide the truth
check.why: A cover-up is an effort to hide the truth. Critics believed officials were hiding what happened to Morgan.

check.q: What did critics point to as signs of a cover-up?
choices: Some officials were Masons, and some trials ended with men acquitted
check.why: The reading says critics noted that some officials were Masons and some trials ended in acquittals.

check.q: Why was it hard for ordinary Masons to show they were innocent?
choices: Their group was secret, so outsiders could not see what they did
check.why: The reading says that when a group is secret, it is hard for members to show outsiders they are innocent.

lessons.title: The Anti-Masonic Party
lessons.mainIdea: Anger over the Morgan case grew into the Anti-Masonic Party, often called the first third party in American history.
reading: In February 1828, Thurlow Weed and Samuel Heron started a newspaper in Rochester, New York. It was called the Anti-Masonic Enquirer. Papers like it told the Morgan story again and again. They helped turn local anger into a political movement.

A *political party* is a group that works to elect its members to office. In those years, most voters chose one of two big parties. The Anti-Masons became a *third party*, a party outside the two main ones. It is often called the first third party in American history.

The party was strongest in New York, Vermont and other northeastern states. Its members wanted Masons kept out of public office. They believed secret oaths did not belong in a free country where the people rule.

Well-known people joined the cause. Former president John Quincy Adams wrote public letters against Masonic oaths from 1831 to 1833. They were later collected in a book, Letters on the Masonic Institution, printed in 1847.

words.d: a group that works to elect its members to public office
a political party outside the two main parties

look.title: A Former President Speaks Out
look.text: Adams argued that the Masonic oaths, with their frightening penalties, were wrong. He said such oaths had no place in a free republic. He called on Masons to give them up.
look.cite: John Quincy Adams, Letters on the Masonic Institution (Boston: T. R. Marvin, 1847), letters written 1831-1833 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: What does Adams want Masons to change? Why would a former president's words carry extra weight?

check.q: What is a third party?
choices: A party held after an election
A political party outside the two main ones
check.why: A third party is a political party outside the two main ones, like the Anti-Masonic Party.

check.q: Who started the Anti-Masonic Enquirer in Rochester?
choices: William Morgan and David C. Miller
John Quincy Adams and William Wirt
check.why: The reading says Thurlow Weed and Samuel Heron started the paper in February 1828.

check.q: What did the Anti-Masons want?
choices: A new canal to Fort Niagara
Masons kept out of public office
check.why: Anti-Masons wanted Masons kept out of public office because they distrusted secret oaths.

lessons.title: The First National Convention
lessons.mainIdea: In 1831 the Anti-Masons held the first national nominating convention, a way of choosing candidates that parties still use.
reading: Today, every four years, the big parties hold national conventions. Crowds cheer. Delegates from every state choose the party's candidate for president. That custom started with the Anti-Masons.

From September 26 to 28, 1831, about 110 *delegates* from 13 states met in Baltimore, Maryland. A delegate is a person sent to speak and vote for others. It was the first national *nominating convention*, a meeting where a party picks its candidate. Before this, small groups of leaders in Congress often chose candidates.

The delegates chose William Wirt for president. Wirt was a lawyer who had served as U.S. attorney general. Surprisingly, he had once been a Mason himself. The convention also issued an Address to the People. Many historians count it as an early party *platform*, a public list of a party's beliefs and plans.

Other parties soon copied the idea and held national conventions of their own. In the 1832 election, Wirt won only one state, Vermont, with its 7 electoral votes. The party lost, but its way of choosing candidates lasted.

words.d: people sent to speak and vote for a larger group
a meeting where a political party picks its candidate
a public list of a political party's beliefs and plans

look.title: The 1832 Presidential Election
look.cite: Electoral vote totals, 1832 presidential election (U.S. National Archives, Electoral College records)
look.prompt: How many electoral votes did Wirt win? Why might a party that won so few votes still matter in history?

check.q: What happens at a nominating convention?
check.why: A nominating convention is a meeting where a party picks its candidate, as the Anti-Masons did in 1831.

check.q: Where and when did the first national nominating convention meet?
check.why: The Anti-Masons met in Baltimore from September 26 to 28, 1831.

check.q: What surprising fact about William Wirt does the reading give?
choices: He had once been a Mason

lessons.title: Lodges Close Their Doors
lessons.mainIdea: After the Morgan affair, hundreds of Masonic lodges closed, especially in New York and Vermont.
reading: Anti-Masonic anger hit lodges hard. Some neighbors stopped speaking to members. Churches and families argued about the lodge. Many men quietly quit. Others kept their membership but stopped meeting.

New York had about 480 lodges in 1826. By the 1830s, only about 75 were still working, by common counts. Sources give different numbers, so historians use the word 'about.' Every lodge in Vermont gave up its *charter*, the official paper that lets a lodge meet. In Kentucky, lodges fell from 66 to 37.

The wave reached Illinois too. The first Grand Lodge of Illinois, formed in 1823, stopped meeting around 1827. It was formed again at Jacksonville in 1840. The Panic of 1837, a money crisis, also made it hard for clubs to survive in these years.

The Anti-Masonic Party faded in the later 1830s. Many of its members joined the new Whig Party. Masonry slowly recovered and grew large again later in the century. Its sharp *decline* after 1826 shows how fast public trust can be lost.

words.d: the official paper that gives a lodge or group the right to meet
a drop in size, strength or numbers

check.why: The reading says New York fell from about 480 lodges to about 75.

lessons.title: Proven and Never Proven
lessons.mainIdea: The Morgan affair shows the difference between what records prove, a kidnapping, and what was never proven, a murder.
reading: In September 1882, a stone monument to William Morgan was dedicated in the cemetery at Batavia. The National Christian Association, a group against secret societies, paid for it. Its words say, as a fact, that Masons murdered him.

A *monument* is a lasting marker that honors a person or event. Monuments can also make a *claim*, a statement that something is true. This monument states something no court ever proved. It tells us what its builders believed 56 years after Morgan vanished.

Here is what records do prove. Morgan was arrested, jailed and taken away by force. Men connected to local lodges were convicted of kidnapping. A national party grew out of the anger. Hundreds of lodges closed.

Here is what was never proven: that Morgan was killed, who killed him, or that the Masonic order as a whole planned it. Keeping these two lists apart is a skill. You can use it every time you read a strong claim about a secret group.

words.d: a lasting marker, often of stone, that honors a person or event
a statement that something is true, which may or may not be proven

chapters.title: Know-Nothings and Anti-Secret Crusaders
chapters.bigQuestion: How did fear of secret groups get turned against ordinary neighbors in the 1800s and early 1900s?

story.title: The March to the Courthouse
story.kicker: In April 1855, a fight over beer licenses in Chicago turns into a clash in the street.
paragraphs: It is April 1855 in Chicago. The city is young, muddy and growing fast. Many of its newest people came from Germany and Ireland. On the North Side, German families gather in beer halls after a long week of work. They talk, sing and drink lager, a kind of beer popular in Germany.

Chicago has a new mayor, Levi Boone. His side won the city election in March with a promise of law and order. The city raised the price of a yearly saloon license from $50 to $300. It also moved to close saloons on Sundays. For many immigrant families, Sunday was the one free day to gather.

Some saloon keepers would not pay. Police arrested them. Their cases came to court on April 21. That day, crowds gathered at the courthouse to support them. More marchers came from the North Side, crossing the Clark Street bridge. Police met them there, and the two sides clashed.

When it was over, one protester was dead and about 60 people had been arrested. People called it the Lager Beer Riot. Behind it was a larger fear. Mayor Boone had been elected with help from a secret order that distrusted Catholic immigrants. Its members were called the Know-Nothings.
story.think: How can a rule that seems to be about one thing, like beer, really be about something bigger?

lessons.title: Newcomers and Old Fears
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1840s and 1850s, many Irish and German immigrants arrived, and nativists feared them, largely because many were Catholic.
reading: In the late 1840s, a terrible famine struck Ireland. The potato crop failed year after year. Hundreds of thousands of Irish people sailed to America. At the same time, many Germans left home after failed revolutions and hard times. Most came to work, raise families and build new lives.

Most Irish immigrants and many German immigrants were Catholic. At that time, most American-born citizens were Protestant. Many Protestants distrusted the Catholic Church. Some claimed, without evidence, that Catholics would obey the pope instead of American laws.

An *immigrant* is a person who moves to a new country to live. The belief that people born in a country deserve more rights than newcomers is called *nativism*. Nativists saw immigrants as a threat to jobs, to elections and to the nation's religion.

In real life, most Irish and German Catholics were ordinary neighbors. They dug canals, built railroads, opened shops and joined churches. The fear did not come from what they did. It came from what others imagined they might do.

words.d: a person who moves to a new country to live
the belief that people born in a country deserve more rights than newcomers

look.title: Two Families on a Dock
look.text: Picture a New York dock in 1850. An Irish family steps off a crowded ship with one trunk. A few feet away, a German couple carries a small child and a bag of tools. Both families are tired and hungry. Both are looking for work and a place to live. Some people watching see new neighbors. Others see a threat.
look.prompt: What do the two families actually want? What might make an onlooker see a threat instead of a neighbor?

choices: The belief that people born in a country deserve more rights than newcomers
check.why: The reading defines nativism as the belief that people born in a country deserve more rights than newcomers.

choices: Many were Catholic, and some claimed Catholics would obey the pope over American law

check.q: According to the reading, what did most Irish and German Catholic immigrants actually do?
choices: Worked, built, opened shops and joined churches
check.why: The reading says they dug canals, built railroads, opened shops and joined churches.

lessons.title: The Order of the Star Spangled Banner
lessons.mainIdea: The Know-Nothings began as a secret, oath-bound order whose members answered questions about it with the words 'I know nothing.'
reading: In 1849, a man named Charles B. Allen started a new society in New York City. He called it the Order of the Star Spangled Banner. The name honored the flag. But the order was not open to everyone. Members had to be native-born Protestant men.

The order was *oath-bound*. Members swore solemn promises to keep its business secret. It had passwords, secret handshakes and levels of membership. When outsiders asked about it, members replied, 'I know nothing.'

The newspaper editor Horace Greeley gave them a nickname: the *Know-Nothings*. The name stuck. Soon the order had lodges in many states. Its members met in secret, but they aimed to win public elections.

There is a sharp *irony* here. Irony is when something turns out the opposite of what you would expect. The Know-Nothings accused Catholics of a secret plot. Yet they were a secret society themselves, with hidden rules and oaths.

words.d: held together by solemn promises that members swear
the nickname for members of the Order of the Star Spangled Banner and the movement it led in the 1850s
when something turns out the opposite of what you would expect

look.title: An Imagined Night in 1854
look.text: A reporter stops a man leaving a hall late at night. What happens in there? the reporter asks. The man tips his hat. I know nothing, he says, and walks away. The reporter writes the answer in his notebook. By morning, half the town is repeating it.
look.prompt: Why would an answer like this make people curious and even more suspicious? How is it like the Masons' secrecy in the Morgan story?

check.q: Who started the Order of the Star Spangled Banner in 1849?
check.why: The reading says Charles B. Allen started the order in New York City in 1849.

check.q: How did the Know-Nothings get their name?
choices: Members answered questions about the order with 'I know nothing'
They refused to go to school
A judge named them in court
check.why: Members answered outsiders with 'I know nothing,' and Horace Greeley turned that into a nickname.

check.q: What is the irony the reading points out?
choices: The order was named after a song
The order started in New York
A secret group accused others of secret plots
check.why: The Know-Nothings accused Catholics of a secret plot while being a secret society themselves.

lessons.title: Know-Nothings in Power
lessons.mainIdea: In the mid-1850s the Know-Nothings, running as the American Party, won big elections, and then the movement faded fast.
reading: In November 1854, Know-Nothing candidates swept Massachusetts. Henry J. Gardner became governor. All but two members of the state *legislature*, the group that makes a state's laws, were Know-Nothings too. The older parties were shocked.
In public, the movement called itself the *American Party*. It wanted immigrants to wait many more years before they could become citizens and vote. It wanted only native-born men to hold office.

Election days could turn violent. On August 6, 1855, in Louisville, Kentucky, mobs of Know-Nothing supporters attacked German and Irish Catholic neighborhoods. About 22 people died. People called it Bloody Monday. The victims were ordinary families, blamed for a plot that did not exist.

In 1856, former president Millard Fillmore ran as the American Party's candidate. He won only one state, Maryland. Soon the movement split over slavery, and it faded away. Its members scattered into other parties within a few years.

words.d: the group of elected people who make a state's or nation's laws
the public name of the Know-Nothing movement when it ran candidates in elections

choices: Know-Nothings won the governor's office and almost the whole legislature

check.why: Henry J. Gardner became governor, and all but two members of the legislature were Know-Nothings.

choices: Election-day attacks on German and Irish Catholic neighborhoods in Louisville

lessons.title: Mayor Boone's New Rules
lessons.mainIdea: In 1855 Chicago elected Levi Boone, whose nativist and temperance coalition raised saloon license fees in a way that hit immigrants hardest.
reading: On March 6, 1855, Chicago voters chose Levi Boone as mayor. His side was a *coalition*, a group of different people who join together for a shared goal. It joined nativists with the *temperance* movement. Temperance means cutting back on alcohol or banning it.

Under Boone, the city raised the yearly saloon *license* from $50 to $300. A license is official permission to do something, like run a business. These licenses had to be renewed every three months. The city also moved to close saloons on Sundays. Supporters said the rules would bring law and order.

Who paid the price? Many saloons and beer halls were run by German and Irish immigrants. Sunday was often the only day working people had free. A fee six times higher could shut down a small family business.
Critics saw the rules as a way to punish immigrants without saying so. Supporters said they only wanted safer, quieter streets. Either way, the rules fell hardest on the city's newest neighbors.

words.d: a group of different people or groups who join together for a shared goal
cutting back on alcohol or banning it
official permission to do something, such as run a business

choices: Cutting back on alcohol or banning it
check.why: The reading defines temperance as cutting back on alcohol or banning it. It was one half of Boone's coalition.

check.why: Under Boone, the yearly fee rose from $50 to $300, six times higher.

choices: Immigrants could not vote at all

check.why: The reading says many saloons and beer halls were run by German and Irish immigrants.

lessons.title: The Lager Beer Riot
lessons.mainIdea: On April 21, 1855, a protest over the license rules became a clash with police in which one man died and about 60 people were arrested.
reading: Some saloon keepers would not pay the new fee. Police arrested them. Their cases came before a judge on April 21, 1855. Their friends and neighbors decided to show support. They planned a *protest*, a public action to show that people disagree.

Crowds gathered at the courthouse. Then more marchers came from the North Side, where many Germans lived. They crossed the Clark Street bridge toward the courthouse. Police were waiting. The two sides clashed, and shots were fired.

When it ended, one protester was dead. About 60 people were arrested. The event is called the Lager Beer Riot. A *riot* is a violent disturbance by a crowd. Lager was the German-style beer served in many beer halls.

Boone served only one year as mayor. In the next election, in 1856, Chicago voters chose a different leader, and the Know-Nothings lost power in the city. Immigrant voters had shown they would stand up for their rights.

words.d: a public action to show that people disagree with something
a violent disturbance by a crowd

look.title: Two Imagined Headlines
look.text: Imagine two Chicago papers the next morning. One headline says: Mob Attacks Police at Clark Street. The other says: Working People Stand Up for Their Rights. Both describe the same day, the same bridge and the same crowd.
look.prompt: What does each headline want readers to feel? What facts would you check before trusting either one?

check.why: Marchers from the North Side crossed the Clark Street bridge, and police met them there.

check.q: What is a riot?
choices: A violent disturbance by a crowd
check.why: The reading defines a riot as a violent disturbance by a crowd.

choices: He moved the city council to Wisconsin

check.why: In the 1856 election Chicago chose a different leader, and the Know-Nothings lost power in the city.

lessons.title: Lincoln's Private Letter
lessons.mainIdea: In 1855 Abraham Lincoln of Illinois wrote privately that he was not a Know-Nothing and that their ideas broke the promise of the Declaration of Independence.
reading: In August 1855, Abraham Lincoln was a lawyer in Springfield, Illinois. He was not yet famous across the nation. On August 24, he wrote a long letter to his close friend Joshua Speed in Kentucky. In it, he said plainly that he was not a Know-Nothing.

Lincoln explained why. He had long said that slavery was wrong. He asked how a person who hated the oppression of Black people could support treating other groups as lesser people. To him, the two kinds of unfairness were connected.

He also imagined how the Know-Nothings would change the *Declaration of Independence*. It says all men are created equal. Lincoln warned that they would add exceptions: Black people, foreigners and Catholics. He meant that nativism broke the nation's founding *principle*.

Lincoln kept these words in a private letter. Historians note that he avoided attacking the Know-Nothings in public. He needed their voters in the fight to stop slavery from spreading. The letter shows what he believed when he was not speaking to a crowd.

words.d: the 1776 document that announced American independence and said all men are created equal
a basic belief or rule that guides what people do

look.title: Lincoln Writes to Joshua Speed
look.text: Lincoln wrote that he was not a Know-Nothing. He asked how anyone who hated the oppression of Black Americans could favor pushing down other groups. If the Know-Nothings took control, he warned, the Declaration would say all men are created equal, except Black people, foreigners and Catholics.
look.cite: Abraham Lincoln to Joshua F. Speed, August 24, 1855, in The Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln, ed. Roy P. Basler, vol. 2 (1953), pp. 320-323 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Which two kinds of unfairness does Lincoln connect? Why might he say this in a private letter instead of a speech?

check.q: To whom did Lincoln write his 1855 letter about the Know-Nothings?
check.why: Lincoln wrote to his close friend Joshua Speed on August 24, 1855.

check.q: Which founding principle did Lincoln say the Know-Nothings would break?
choices: That all men are created equal
check.why: Lincoln warned they would add exceptions to the Declaration's promise that all men are created equal.

check.q: Why did Lincoln avoid attacking the Know-Nothings in public, according to historians?
choices: He needed their voters in the fight to stop slavery from spreading

check.why: Historians note he needed Know-Nothing voters in the fight against the spread of slavery.

lessons.title: Jonathan Blanchard of Wheaton
lessons.mainIdea: Jonathan Blanchard, the first president of Wheaton College, spent decades arguing that every kind of secret society was wrong.
reading: Jonathan Blanchard was a minister, a teacher and an *abolitionist*, a person who worked to end slavery. Before coming to Wheaton, he led Knox College in Galesburg, Illinois. In 1860 he became the first president of Wheaton College, west of Chicago.

Blanchard believed secret societies did harm. He opposed the Masons, the Odd Fellows and every other *secret order*. His reasons were religious and political. He believed Christians should not swear secret oaths. He also believed a free country needed open, public dealing.
Blanchard was different from the Know-Nothings. They targeted Catholic immigrants. He aimed at all secret lodges, whatever their members' faith or birthplace. His fight was against secrecy itself.

Lodge members strongly disagreed with him. They said their orders raised money for widows, cared for the sick and taught good character. They saw Blanchard as attacking good neighbors. You can weigh both views.

words.d: a person who worked to end slavery
a society whose members promise to keep its ceremonies or business private

look.title: An Imagined Talk at a Church Supper
look.text: At a church supper in 1870, a Wheaton student says: My teacher says secret oaths have no place in a free country. An older farmer answers: My lodge paid for my brother's funeral when nobody else would help. Both are sure they are right.
look.prompt: What does each speaker value? Which view does Blanchard hold, and what would a lodge member say back to him?

check.q: Which college did Blanchard lead as its first president in 1860?
check.why: Blanchard became Wheaton College's first president in 1860, after leading Knox College.

check.q: How was Blanchard different from the Know-Nothings?
choices: He opposed all secret lodges, not one faith or group of immigrants
He wanted to join the Masons
check.why: The Know-Nothings targeted Catholic immigrants, while Blanchard opposed every secret lodge.

check.q: What did lodge members say in their own defense?
choices: They helped widows, cared for the sick and taught good character
check.why: The reading says members pointed to their help for widows and the sick and their lessons in character.

lessons.title: The Christian Cynosure
lessons.mainIdea: From 1868, Blanchard's National Christian Association in Chicago published the Christian Cynosure to campaign against secret societies.
reading: In 1868, Blanchard helped found the National Christian Association. Its headquarters were in Chicago. Its goal was to warn Americans against secret societies of every kind. A *campaign* like this is an organized effort to reach a goal over time.

The association published a newspaper called the Christian Cynosure, and Blanchard edited it. A *cynosure* is a guiding light, like the star that sailors steer by. For decades, the paper printed arguments, letters and reports against lodges.

The association also kept the Morgan story alive. In 1882 it paid for the Morgan Monument in Batavia, New York. More than fifty years after Morgan vanished, the monument named Masons as his killers, a claim no court had proved.

All this made Illinois a center of the movement against secret societies. Blanchard's papers and the association's records are kept today in the Wheaton College Archives. Students and researchers can still study them.

words.d: an organized effort to reach a goal over time
a guiding light, like the star sailors steer by; also something everyone looks to

look.title: Imagining One Stack of Papers
look.text: Picture a stack of the Christian Cynosure on a table in Chicago. One page retells the Morgan case from 1826. Another prints a letter from a man explaining why he left his lodge. A third asks readers to help pay for a monument in Batavia.
look.prompt: How could one newspaper keep a fifty-year-old story alive? What would you want to check before trusting one of its reports?

check.q: Where was the National Christian Association based?
check.why: The reading says the association's headquarters were in Chicago.

check.q: What does cynosure mean?
choices: A guiding light, like the star sailors steer by
check.why: A cynosure is a guiding light, like the star sailors steer by. The paper hoped to guide its readers.

check.q: How did the association keep the Morgan story alive?
choices: It closed the lodges in Vermont
It paid for the 1882 Morgan Monument
check.why: The National Christian Association paid for the Morgan Monument in Batavia in 1882.

lessons.title: The Knights of Columbus
lessons.mainIdea: The Knights of Columbus began in 1882 as a Catholic fraternal order that helped families, especially widows and children.
reading: In the early 1880s, Father Michael J. McGivney was an assistant pastor at St. Mary's Church in New Haven, Connecticut. He saw families fall into poverty when a working father died. He wanted to help.

In October 1881, he and a group of Catholic men formed a new society. On March 29, 1882, the Connecticut legislature granted it a charter. They named it the Knights of Columbus. It was a *fraternal order*, a brotherhood whose members help one another. It also offered life *insurance*, so a family would get money if the father died.

The Catholic Church did not allow Catholics to join the Masons. Many other lodges had a Protestant feel. The Knights gave Catholic men a lodge of their own, with ceremonies, charity and friendship. The order spread fast. Chicago Council No. 182, the first in Illinois, began in 1896.

Like other lodges, the Knights had private ceremonies. That privacy made them a target. Some people who already feared Catholics imagined the Knights were hiding a plot. The next lesson shows how that fear was used.

words.d: a brotherhood whose members help one another
a plan that pays money to a person or family after a loss, such as a death

look.title: A Kitchen in New Haven
look.text: Picture a New Haven kitchen in 1882. A mother sits at the table with three children. Her husband worked in a factory, and he died last month. In 1882 there is little help from the government. A letter arrives from the Knights with money from his insurance.
look.prompt: How would that money change this family's future? Why might Catholic men want to join an order like this?

check.q: Who founded the Knights of Columbus?
check.why: Father Michael J. McGivney of St. Mary's Church in New Haven founded the Knights.

check.q: What is a fraternal order?
choices: A brotherhood whose members help one another
check.why: The reading defines a fraternal order as a brotherhood whose members help one another.

check.q: Why did the Knights offer life insurance?
choices: So a family would get money if the father died
check.why: McGivney saw families fall into poverty when a father died, so the Knights offered insurance.

lessons.title: A Fake Oath Before Congress
lessons.mainIdea: A forged Knights of Columbus oath was printed in the Congressional Record in 1913 only as evidence, and a House committee condemned it as false.
reading: In 1912, Eugene Bonniwell ran for Congress in Pennsylvania and lost to Thomas Butler. Bonniwell challenged the result. His papers pointed to a false document that had been spread during the race.
That document was a *forgery*, a fake made to look real. It claimed to be the secret oath of the Knights of Columbus. It falsely said members swore to harm Protestants. No such oath was real.

A House committee studied the case. Its report was printed in the *Congressional Record*, the official record of what happens in Congress, on February 15, 1913. The fake oath was printed there too, but only as an *exhibit*, a piece of evidence in the case.

The committee did not stop there. It said it could not condemn the fake oath strongly enough. It called the document *libel*, false writing that harms someone's good name. Congress had named the oath a fake.

words.d: a fake made to look real
the official record of what is said and done in Congress
a document or object shown as evidence in a case
false writing that harms someone's good name

look.title: What the Committee Said
look.text: The committee wrote that it could not condemn too strongly the printing of the false and libelous article, which was the spurious Knights of Columbus oath.
look.cite: House Committee on Elections No. 1, report on Bonniwell v. Butler, Congressional Record, February 15, 1913, p. 3215 and following (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Which words does the committee use to describe the oath? The word spurious means fake. What does the committee's choice of words tell you?

check.q: What is a forgery?
choices: A fake made to look real
check.why: A forgery is a fake made to look real, like the false Knights of Columbus oath.

check.q: Why was the fake oath printed in the Congressional Record?
choices: Only as an exhibit, a piece of evidence in an election case
Because Congress believed it was real
To honor the Knights of Columbus
To help Bonniwell win a new election
check.why: The reading says the oath appeared only as an exhibit in the Bonniwell v. Butler case.

check.q: What did the House committee say about the oath?
choices: It was the true oath of the Knights
It should be taught in schools
check.why: The committee condemned the oath as false and called it libel.

lessons.title: Copied from the Record
lessons.mainIdea: Pamphlet makers reprinted the fake oath with the label 'Copied from the Congressional Record,' hiding the fact that Congress had called it false.
reading: After 1913, anti-Catholic *pamphlets*, or short printed booklets, began to reprint the fake oath. Many carried a proud label: Copied from the Congressional Record, Feb. 15, 1913. In a narrow way the label was true. The words really had appeared there.

What the label left out was the *context*, the facts around something that give it meaning. The pamphlets did not say the oath was printed as evidence of a lie. They did not say the committee condemned it. Readers were meant to think Congress stood behind it.
This is a *misleading* use of a source. Each word on the label may be true, but the reader walks away with a false idea. Even today, people quote real documents out of context to spread fear.

Think back over this unit. Morgan's disappearance made neighbors suspect every Mason. The Know-Nothings made neighbors suspect every Catholic immigrant. The fake oath did the same to Catholic Knights. Each time, fear of a secret group landed on real people who had done nothing wrong.

words.d: short printed booklets, often meant to persuade people
the facts around something that give it meaning
giving a false idea, even when some of the words are true

look.title: Reading a Pamphlet Closely
look.text: A pamphlet printed after 1913 has big letters across the top: Copied from the Congressional Record, Feb. 15, 1913. Below them is the fake oath. Nowhere does the pamphlet say that a House committee called the oath false and libelous in that same report.
look.prompt: What is true about the label? What does it hide? Write one sentence that would give readers the missing context.

check.q: What is context?
choices: The facts around something that give it meaning
check.why: The reading defines context as the facts around something that give it meaning.

check.q: Why was the label 'Copied from the Congressional Record' misleading?
choices: The words never appeared in the Record
The Record did not exist in 1913
The label was printed in German
It hid that the committee had condemned the oath as false
check.why: The words did appear in the Record, but the label hid that the committee called the oath false.

check.q: What pattern does the reading find across the unit?
choices: Fear of secret groups landed on real people who had done nothing wrong
Every secret society was a criminal gang
Secret groups never faced any critics
check.why: The reading says fear of Masons, Catholics and the Knights each landed on neighbors who had done nothing wrong.

review.q: Why were members of the Order of the Star Spangled Banner called Know-Nothings?
choices: They said 'I know nothing' when asked about the order
review.why: Members answered outsiders with 'I know nothing,' and the nickname stuck.

review.q: Which event happened in Chicago in 1855?
choices: The founding of the Knights of Columbus
review.why: The Lager Beer Riot took place in Chicago on April 21, 1855. Bloody Monday was in Louisville.

review.q: How were the Know-Nothings and Jonathan Blanchard different?
choices: The Know-Nothings targeted Catholic immigrants; Blanchard opposed all secret lodges
The Know-Nothings opposed all secret orders; Blanchard opposed only Catholics
review.why: The Know-Nothings aimed at Catholic immigrants, while Blanchard fought secrecy in every lodge.

review.q: Which Illinois lawyer wrote privately in 1855 that he was not a Know-Nothing?
review.why: Abraham Lincoln wrote this to Joshua Speed on August 24, 1855.

review.q: What did Mayor Boone's coalition join together?
choices: Abolitionists and the Knights of Columbus
review.why: Boone's coalition joined nativists with people who wanted to limit alcohol.

review.q: What is the best way to describe the Knights of Columbus oath of 1913?
choices: A real oath that Congress approved
A forgery that a House committee condemned
A rule of the Order of the Star Spangled Banner
review.why: The oath was a forgery, and the House committee called it false and libelous.

review.q: Which question would best check a pamphlet labeled 'Copied from the Congressional Record'?
choices: Why was it printed in the Record, and what did Congress say about it?
How many pages does the pamphlet have?
review.why: Asking why it was printed and what Congress said brings back the missing context.

review.q: Who was hurt most by the fears in this chapter?
review.why: The chapter shows fear landing on Catholic and immigrant families in Chicago, Louisville and beyond.
